content.overview: Traceability connects source and destination while genealogy explains transformations. Both require stable identifiers, event records and controlled corrections.

vocabulary.definition: Following material from a downstream unit toward its sources and process history.
Following source material toward downstream lots, units, samples or destinations.
Recorded split, merge, conversion or association that changes material relationships.

sections.title: Identifiers anchor events
sections.body: Stable lot and unit IDs should persist even when names, packages or locations change.

sections.title: Transformations need explicit relationships
sections.body: Splits, merges, rework and samples should preserve parent-child links so scope can be reconstructed.

sections.title: Corrections retain history
sections.body: Data changes should identify who changed what, when and why without obscuring the original record.

workedExamples: One drying lot becomes three package lots and two lab samples; every child remains linked to the parent and relevant process history.
commonMistakes: Using a cultivar nickname as the lot ID.
Overwriting a parent ID after repackaging.
Correcting a record without reason or audit trail.
content.practicalApplication: Create a genealogy diagram and event table for a harvest that splits, merges under an authorized rule, is sampled and is packaged.
content.summary: Traceability is strongest when durable IDs and explicit genealogy events preserve both direction and history.
